utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you moved towards Bratunac, you didn't really know what your new assignment in that new location would be?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware at any moment that already on the 11th of July, the VRS had entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: When we came to Bratunac, we knew that there were combat activities going on. Whether Srebrenica had fallen or not, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning of the 12th, you moved to carry out your combat assignment, correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, was it foggy that morning? Was that the reason why you didn't move before 8.00?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that emerging at Budak village you would be ending up in an area where you could enter into combat with the BH army and that there was a possible presence of the BH army there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: We were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you moved -- why you advanced so slowly coming into that area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier today, you stated that you were moving towards Budak village. My question was how deep did you go into those hills looking from the road, the asphalt road, leading to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether moving on your assignment, you saw just behind the Yellow Bridge, you saw a UN check-point?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: There was something, a structure, I believe it was a check-point, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally or your platoon have any orders to disarm or capture the members of the Dutch Battalion who were located there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, can you tell us how long this assignment of yours lasted? How long did you move into the hills towards Budak village?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know precisely. Perhaps an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point you received orders to stop and that your entire unit should descend on to the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Right. When we arrived up there at that point, we stayed there for an hour, maybe two, and then we drew back on to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant to ask you. Could you tell us more precisely that point where you descended on to the road, how far was it from the place where you saw the majority of the civilian population gathered?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Maybe 600, maybe 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you climb down to the asphalt road walking along a macadam road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now look at Exhibit 4D101 that we have used before? While it is called up on e-court, let me say that it's a map of this area, Bratunac, Yellow Bridge, Potocari, the road towards Srebrenica, and maybe the witness could mark the direction of his unit's movement on that morning of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you will see a map soon on the screen, and if you can orient yourself on that map, maybe you could mark for us the direction in which you moved. At the same time, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher assist us and give a pen to the witness? Could we zoom in on the Bratunac area? That's the central part of the map, at the crossroad of these two asphalt roads? Thank you. Could you scroll down a bit? You will see Potocari. Down. That's right. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I will try to direct you. Do you see on this sketch an area marked Borici? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just below there is an interruption in the road. It looks like a bridge. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see down the road the area of Budak village?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the area where it says Pecista and letters TV, standing for "tvornica" I suppose, factory?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this enough to orient you now so you can mark the route you used from Zuti Most towards Budak and where you emerged on the road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Well, we went along this part of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can use the pen to draw on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: [Marks] And then we turned somewhere, at this point, and we came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the area where you stayed for about two hours, as you said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you said you walked along a macadam road down towards the road. Can you mark that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark where most of that civilian population you could see from the hills were located? Could you put a circle?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Here, I think. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please mark the area from the point you emerged from the road to this circle, could you just write 600 metres and M for metres?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on the right-hand side anywhere you like, put today's date, please, and your signature.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And your signature, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we leave this on the screen for the next couple of questions? And then we'll remove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, can we please correct something? It says 28th of July. Today we are 28th of June. I would kindly ask the usher to assist us with erasing that erroneous date and replacing it by the correct date, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can that still be done? You need to show him how to erase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the witness and the usher. I don't think her assistance will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, how long did you stay on the road, on this asphalt road, before you started moving towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: We stayed there while we were being gathered, waiting for the vehicle to come and pick us up. I believe we were there for an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the way from the place where you had gathered, to Sandici, where you stopped, did you make any stops in Bratunac, for example?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember actually. We might have. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, we put it to you that the 2nd Detachment Sekovici left the area of Potocari before the evacuation of the civilian population of Potocari started. To your best recollection, would you agree that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally did not see the moment when the transport of the civilians from Potocari started in the direction of Tuzla while were you in Potocari, that is?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you were leaving the area of Potocari to go towards Bratunac, on your left-hand side you again passed the check-point of the Dutch Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: The left-hand side, the right-hand side -- we did pass it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No members of your unit opened fire or stopped to disarm members of the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we are moving to the territory of Sandici, I believe that we will no longer need this photo and it can be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Save it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To your best recollection, Mr. Celic, on the 12th of July, in the afternoon, when did you arrive and when were you deployed along the Sandici-Kravica road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, indeed, but I don't know how late it was. Maybe it was around 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You already found there some members of the VRS and members of the 1st Company of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some people there but I don't know who they were, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what military unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, by the way, bearing in mind the answer that you provided to my learned friend, Mr. Thayer, you had overalls and two-piece uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had overalls and we also had two-piece uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that two-piece uniform also a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it was also olive-drab?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your belts were not white, were they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, they were not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons that you mentioned, the M-84 machine-gun that you were issued was calibre 7.62 made in 64 [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, page 52, line 6, the model was made in 84 rather than in 64, just to avoid any misunderstandings. I don't think that this is very important but I would just like for the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's on the record now. So let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether on the 12th of July, i.e., during that afternoon and the night between the 12th and the 13th, there were any prisoners within the area that you might have controlled?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that afternoon or during that night, was there any shooting from the direction of the forest that was ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting coming from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the afternoon on the 12th of July, you saw the population being transported in buses and lorries in large numbers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this continue on the 13th as well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your unit did not have anything to do with the transport of the civilians, did it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was your attention drawn to the fact that a column of the 28th Division of the BiH army was moving along the open spaces and through the forests ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: We were told that up there, there were men, but nobody mentioned any numbers or names of any units, so I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were told that they were members of the BiH army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you this: Do you remember that next to these vehicles on the road, did you see an armoured vehicle of the United Nations, who also followed the same road?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time during the war and your membership in the 2nd Detachment of Sekovici see your unit using a bull horn for the purposes similar to those that you described today?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your best recollection, did your unit have any such device at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your chief examination, you have explained in detail the passage of the prisoners that was moving alongside on the road. Can you remember approximately what was the time of -- on that day, the 13th of July, when they passed through there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: It may have been around 2.00 or maybe 3.00. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not recognise any escorts of the column?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know now is this: At the moment when that column had passed, did you already have information that you were supposed to abandon the area and to eventually head for Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were stories to that effect. We have been -- we were told that we should leave the area quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody said about the people in the column actually having been prisoners that were taken when the crowd moved out of the forest?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question? I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, that column of prisoners was passing by you, they were on foot and they were moving down the road. Among you, members of your unit, were there any words about the origin of these prisoners? Did anybody say that these were men who had come out of the forest?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that those were the same men, those who had come out of the forest. I assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody say that some of them had thrown their arms, that they were unarmed at the moment that -- when they were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were such stories. After some time people did say that these men had thrown their arms and that they came out of the woods. At certain moments, there were conflicts in the forest, although there were no members of our army or our police up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on that day, on the 13th of July, General Mladic also appeared in the area? Were there stories to that effect amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. I heard that he'd been here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally didn't see him, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that on the 13th of July, late in the afternoon, you left this area and started moving towards Zvornik, i.e., towards Konjevic Polje. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I say, bearing in mind that this was during the summer, that this was between 8.00 and 9.00, would that be approximately the time when you left the area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would approximately be the time when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that another unit replaced you on the road in the positions that you had held up to then? Are you aware of any such unit arriving?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, some men did arrive. I don't know which unit that was, where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have described for us the place where you were billeted the night after, that this was in the area of Konjevic Polje. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of facilities are we talking about? What kind of houses were those where were you billeted?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Houses. By the road. They were there, half demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were abandoned houses, then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that those houses were 300 to 400 metres from the crossroads in the centre of Konjevic Polje in the direction of Zvornik on the right-hand side of the road? That would be the approximate location of these houses, will you agree with me, as you're looking in the direction of Zvornik on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Possibly, or maybe some 200 metres, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That night, between the 13th and 14th of July, were there any combat activities in the area where you were billeted?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were saying that you did not remember that members of the Skelani Platoon were there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you remember, is it possible that in the house where you were, did your commander come to that house, Commander Rado Cuturic, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: It is possible that he came to that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The story about the incident in Kravica that you related to my learned friend, Mr. Thayer, who told you that? Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Konjevic Polje, there were stories to that effect, describing what had taken place, what had transpired. I don't know exactly who told me that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next time when you saw Rado, was it in Zvornik, Baljkovica or further afield? Do you remember when you saw him, were his hands injured? Did he have any visible traces of the injuries?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: His hand was dressed. I don't know which one. I don't know whether it was his left or his right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that he was not with you in Baljkovica when that combat was taking place?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I am confused about one day, about the 14th of July, which escapes me somehow. I would like to establish a chronology backwards. It is the fact that you were wounded on the 16th of July in Baljkovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember to the best of your recollection, how many nights you had spent in Baljkovica, before you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: One night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you should have arrived in Baljkovica on the 15th, in the afternoon, wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you that on the 14th of July, and during the night between the 14th and 15th of July, you arrived in the suburbs of Zvornik in the area of Drinjaca and that you spent that time there waiting your further orders, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: It is possible but I can't remember that at all. I really can't remember where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that before your arrival in Baljkovica you had any combat engagement that you engaged in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No. We spent the entire day of the 15th in Zvornik. We were in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 15th, when was it when you started to go towards Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: It was sometime late in the afternoon. When we arrived it was raining very heavily. We were as wet as mice, as our people like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since a majority of us do not know the area, I will kindly ask you to portray a picture for us. The place where you were between Sandici and Kravica, how far is it from Konjevic Polje and the place where you arrived on the 13th in the evening and where you were billeted that night?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: The place where you were on the 12th and the 13th of July, which is the area between Kravica and Sandici that you have described for us, and I'm going to show you a photo later, how far is that place in kilometres from the place where you spent the night between the 13th and the 14th of July in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: How far is it? Maybe 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us, please, the area where you were billeted in Konjevic Polje between the 13th and 14th of July, how far is that from the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Approximately 35 kilometres, maybe 40 even.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I would like to know is this: In your best knowledge, do you know that parts of the Sekovici Detachment on the 14th of July, did they have any combat missions on their way to Mount Mudrize [phoen] that's in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, in the afternoon, you arrived in Baljkovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, as far as you can remember, were there members of any other police forces that had arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: There was the 1st Company. I don't know whether there were any other detachments. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the 1st Company --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What's --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we are on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, then, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one thing. When you say the 1st Company, do you mean the 1st Company of the PJP, which is part of the centre of security of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there different military formations there in addition to your units?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that afternoon on the 15th and during the following night, did you have any combat engagements?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we arrived later on the 15th, we were deployed, there was a macadam road in that area. In the place where I was, there was a crossroads and men who were there, the troops that were there, told us that there were self-propelled combat pieces in front of us and that the Muslims had kidnapped those pieces. There was some shooting - but not any major ones - sometime in the evening. And this lasted until 4.00 or 5.00. A few -- actually one bullet was fired at that time. I don't know whether that was a signal of some short. They shouted, "Allahu Akbar," and then fierce fighting started, which continued for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was raining. Are you talking about that night, the night between the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we heard more than a few testimonies about this inclement weather, was it really that bad and did it really affect the intensity?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that but it was raining buckets. That was that night. The next day, as far as I remember, there was no rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What time -- at what point on the 16th of July were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time, but the fighting started early in the morning, around 4.00 or 5.00, and then you lose track. Maybe it was 10.00, maybe it was 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, in the afternoon, or in the morning of the 16th, did you see Ljubomir Borovcanin in that area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember hearing that he was somewhere in that area?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a possibility. Maybe people were talking. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we have only one more exhibit that I want to show to this witness, and a couple of more questions that will take ten more minutes, perhaps could we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got the following suggestion to make. First, will there be a re-examination based on what you've haired so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not so far, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the interpreters, technicians and everyone else accept to go on for a further ten minutes after which we will then adjourn? I see Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe Mr. Lazarevic, we wanted to talk a bit about tomorrow and that would be better if we took a break so we could talk about it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. McCloskey, so let's have a break now for 25 -- would 25 minutes be enough for you, Mr. McCloskey, or do you require 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Twenty-five is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To try to make it quick, Mr. Celic, you remember that document from the hospital in Zvornik shown you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw there was your name there in one line and no information about any injuries you sustained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to show it again. Just want to ask you what kind of injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: An entry and exit gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, were you transferred from the Zvornik hospital to a hospital in Milici?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I was transferred from Zvornik to Standard, and after a while I was transferred on to Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And your treatment was completed at the hospital in Milici; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In conclusion, let me ask you, I suppose that from 1993 and until the end of the war, 1995, your Sekovici Detachment participated in a lot of fighting where your units were commanded by Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What are your impressions about Ljubomir Borovcanin as a superior officer, as a human being?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: I can say that very briefly. He was a good man and a strict superior. That means he was kind to people, and he was friendly and helped people whenever he could, when we were at ease, and in combat we had to follow the rules strictly. He insisted on that and people appreciated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Celic. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Djordje Sarapa and I represent Mr. Pandurevic. I have only one question. Do you know if anybody from the Sekovici Detachment was killed at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG CELIC
utterances.text: Let me think. Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, we have no further questions for you, which means that your testimony ends here. You're free to go and you'll be escorted out of the courtroom and receive all the assistance you need to return home. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal for having come over to give testimony and on behalf of everyone present here I wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we circulated a revised witness list last night and as I look at the list, I believe the first item is already admitted, which is -- exhibit list, yes. Yes. So I'm referring to the revised exhibit list that was circulated last night. The first number 1891, I believe has already been admitted, as 1DP01891, and the two video stills, I would submit we should follow the practice that we've engaged in, which is they are part of the video still binder that we are gradually filling and that they be marked for identification until the end of the road, at which time we'll move the entire video still binder into evidence. For the time being we've identified the time on the video at which those photographs can be located as well as the chapter and page from that still binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from any of the Defence teams? None. So that's how it will be. First one, 65 ter number 1891 understanding is that it has already been admitted. Okay. There is one document that the Borovcanin Defence team wishes to tender, and that's 65 ter number 4DIC136, which is a map of the Zvornik area marked by the witness, no objection, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine there are any objections from any of the other Defence teams so that is admitted and we have concluded with this witness. Yes? I understand that you wish to address the Chamber on what's going to happen tomorrow? Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may address the Trial Chamber, I would like to move the Trial Chamber for reconsideration of yesterday's ruling. If Your Honours remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which ruling, that we will have a debate tomorrow, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were instructed yesterday, both the Defence and the Prosecution, to prepare the debate on the issue of the admissibility of Mr. Borovcanin's interview and it was scheduled for tomorrow, for Friday. And in particular the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin is instructed to make a formal request in this respect for tomorrow. After having second thoughts about all this, we have some issue that we would like to raise before the Trial Chamber before we start all this. It is our understanding that the Prosecution wishes to tender Mr. Borovcanin's interviews into evidence through their witness, Mr. Alistair Graham, and according to the latest witness list that we received yesterday, it is his testimony scheduled for the 17th of July. We believe that if Mr. Borovcanin's Defence makes a submission before Mr. Graham's examination-in-chief, it would put itself in rather unfavourable position. Most of the Defence arguments in support of exclusion of Mr. Borovcanin's interview from the evidence are directly relevant and related to the conduct of Mr. Alistair Graham during this interview, not just Mr. Graham but also to some other participants in these interviews. So if we make a full submission about all the topics that we would like to cover in our arguments, we would basically disclose to the Prosecution all our lines of cross-examination which we intend to go with Mr. Graham, we would give them all our tactics, we would practically put ourselves in a situation to give to the Prosecution all our questions even before Mr. Graham takes the stand. And we don't believe it would be fair, that would give huge advantage to the Prosecution over the Defence in such a situation, and it would cause an unfairness towards Mr. Borovcanin's Defence. However, we would like to suggest the Trial Chamber apply the same approach as it did in the similar situation in this particular proceedings, namely the intercept approach. We suggest that we first hear the evidence of Mr. Graham, then after Mr. Graham gives his evidence, and of course, including examination-in-chief, Mr. Borovcanin's interviews could be marked for identification and then we will be in a position to make a full argumentation about the admissibility of his interviews. That's one of the solutions that we might suggest. It was already applied once in these proceedings. I discussed this issue with some of my colleagues in various other cases. I was also instructed that in Milutinovic case, same approach was applied, first to hear the evidence of a witness, who was -- Mr. Graham was one of the participants in this interview, and after he gives his evidence then we will discuss all this. I discussed this issue with Mr. McCloskey earlier this morning. He did have some sympathy, I don't wish to say that he will fully support but he had some sympathies, he said, "I really don't feel good about knowing your cross-examination in advance." That is something like this. But if there are any legal issues that will not be of this importance, which will not be raised by examination of Mr. Graham, then this is something that we can discuss tomorrow. Basically, I hope I stated his position clearly and that basically was it. By now I managed to find only two legal issues which I can discuss tomorrow without putting myself in such a situation to disclose my cross-examination. And these two are whether the Prosecution is obliged to ask for formal admittance of Mr. Borovcanin's interview on Rule 65 ter list. The other issue is, well, it is of course relevant for Mr. Borovcanin's Defence but it's also relevant for all other defences and that's the impact that the admissibility of -- the admission of Mr. Borovcanin's interview into evidence will have towards other Defences. So these are two topics which I can cover tomorrow without any problem. For all the rest, I believe that it would be fair to first cross-examine Mr. Graham and then, depending on his answers that I receive during cross-examination, I will be able to locate other topics which I can then elaborate more after he finishes his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing that is not clear from your submission is what's going to happen in the meantime relating to the use of the interview, which I suppose is video-taped. No? It's not videotaped?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Audio only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. I see. What's going to happen with that? And are you suggesting that, pending the resolution of -- the ultimate resolution of admissibility of this previous -- of this interview with your client, it will not be made use during the testimony of Mr. Graham or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that I -- of course, it has to be used during cross-examination of Mr. Graham. So once Mr. Graham comes, it can -- it has to be used during his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I just simply want to avoid the situation to give my questions in advance to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear because it's of course important and it has -- such a situation has arisen before, as you know, not only in the Milutinovic case but also in others. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. As you know, my biggest concern about this was whether there would be a delay, a legal issue that would result in a delay to the testimony. Since Mr. Lazarevic is not having a problem with the introduction or the offering, that particular problem is -- does not appear to be a problem any more. So I think that is settled, mostly, though there may be some other smaller issues related to another point he said. But before I get to that, I do think the Defence is required to provide, at least the legal grounds by which their cross-examination will take. The Prosecution, while the law is not absolutely clear in our jurisdiction, what I think is clear is that the Prosecution is obligated to provide evidence to the Court that this -- any statements such as this was done according to the rules and was not done in an environment that it would be less than voluntary or it was coercive or inducements or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, and the burden of proof of that lies with you and not with Mr. Lazarevic. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. So that's one of the reasons why we would call Alistair Graham. The Court may be aware of the recent case of Halilovic, the Appellate Chamber allowed the transcript of an interview to come in based on the fact that the transcript itself met those basic criteria, then they threw it out on other grounds. But in any event, we don't wish to try to bring in the transcript without Alistair Graham. Alistair Graham is available and so we would do that. Now, counsel has said that his grounds -- something to do with the way Mr. Graham conducted the interview, so I think we at the very least need to know if he's suggesting that there were inducements, that something happened that caused it to be involuntary. What are the legal grounds by which he is referring to? I don't need, nor do I want, his cross-examination questions but I think we owe -- we are at least owed if -- basically if he's going to try to have this statement thrown out on what must be voluntary grounds at this point, I don't know what other grounds there are, we need to know what they are. Is it inducement, is it voluntary, is it -- what is it? The record itself is very clear. He gets his rights, there's no problems with any disagreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Skip that. Skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's made some allegations here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to hear submissions on something that needs -- that will be discussed later on. For the time being I think what we need to know is Mr. Lazarevic's position on what you have just suggested, namely that at least you should have an initial indication of what he is contesting, what he is contesting you. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just -- one slight other point. It's also very clear not contested that I played a significant role in this interview, and so if there are some sorts of challenges on these undefined as yet subjects, I need to know that as well. It may be more appropriate if there is some kind of allegations that Mr. Thayer handle this. Right now, I was planning on handling it but I don't generally handle things if my involvement could be at issue. I really don't know what he's referring to. So if we could get at least a legal reference. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That raises another point obviously, whether you should be present when we are receiving evidence or submissions on this because if you see yourself even potentially, even if it is a remote possibility, as a witness, then you know what your responsibilities are, and I don't think I need to elaborate on that. This is ordinary -- something which we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My bar association requires me that if I have to become a witness, that I set aside. But for all the years I've been in this business, I will take part in interviews but I will always have an investigator present so I don't see any situation that would require myself to be a witness. If I did see that, I would remove myself. But again, let's -- if we could get more definition on this, we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I mentioned that because I think it's relevant. Then it's up to you, of course. Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With all due respect, and if I can just intervene, I think there are very significant legal issues that the Court has to address, well before we start discussing whether this interview may or may not be admitted into evidence. Specifically, without divulging it, I think Mr. McCloskey will agree with me, the witness who was interviewed in two separate occasions on a couple of days was referred to as a possible suspect. Now, if we look at our rules of evidence and procedure here, they specifically outline -- well the accused, right, at that point. The accused who gave the interview was identified both on the second page of the February 2002 interview and the March 2002 interview, was told that he's possibly a suspect. Now we've seen other interviews that came in and they were either a witness or a suspect and we have seen some variations during those interviews. The rules, specifically 43 and 63, set forth those procedures and guidelines on how to conduct recorded interviews for either suspects or accused and incorporate other requirements from Rule 42(A)(iii), so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. With all due respect to Mr. McCloskey, I think there are very significant issues, although I would join it, I thought the Court addressed the question specifically to Mr. Lazarevic. I want to be involved in the discussion in this. I haven't been given additional copies of transcripts, although I was promised it today that we should get it tomorrow, because there is some revisions from things that were not necessarily heard. They are important. We have to address that and I think both Mr. Alistair, and possibly Mr. McCloskey but I don't think so, should address that as a fundamental threshold, and then at a subsequent time we can determine the issues that Mr. McCloskey is deciding so I think it's a two-prong process, quite candidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear what Mr. Lazarevic has to say before I give you back the floor, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, thank you, Your Honour. I can understand my colleague's concerns regarding all this. I really feel the same. I would have felt the same way if I were in his position, but I have to say I can name all the issues, that it's not something that I cannot do tomorrow, but elaborating more on all these issues would be simply opening all my cards to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's fine. I don't think anyone is going to disagree with you. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make a couple of observations really in relation to what my learned friends representing the co-accused have said? Mr. Lazarevic has suggested that one of the things we could do tomorrow is analyse the effect that this interview would have evidentially against the co-accused. In my submission that would be the wrong thing to do tomorrow. Realistically, the Court first has to decide whether this interview is going to be admitted into evidence. Once that's been done, then the point that Mr. Lazarevic has made does need to be addressed, indeed I've discussed it with a number of my learned friends and indeed with Mr. McCloskey. Presently there is no agreement on the point, and in due course, those of us representing the co-accused will need to know in terms, whether this interview, if admitted into evidence, in part or in whole, has any evidential effect as against our clients. So it is a live issue but it's not one that we should address tomorrow, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will take it that if you have copies of this interview or if you will have copies of this interview, complete copy by today, then you yourselves should be in a position to know how much and to what extent any of the other co-accused are involved in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, frankly I meant more as a matter of theoretical legal principle rather than the actuality of what Mr. Borovcanin said during the course of the interview, because even theoretically, it has a certain knock-on effect as against all the co-accused. If it's only, for example, in relation to the crime base, which clearly he was asked about at some length in the course of the interview. So it's more a theoretical point. I know that other Trial Chambers of the Tribunal have addressed the issue and are addressing the issue. I know as well that it was a live issue in the Blagojevic-Jokic case and indeed I hope Mr. McCloskey will forgive me for saying this but in that case he conceded that Jokic's interview had no evidential effect as against Blagojevic. He said that in terms in the course of a motion. However he has said to me this morning, to be fair to him, that he might resile from that position. It is an issue but it's not one we should address tomorrow and it's complicated, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I definitely would agree to you because what -- I understand you better now what obviously Mr. Josse is referring to is the rule that one finds in several jurisdictions, including my own, and I would imagine also in yours, as to whether if at all and to what extent any statement made by one of the co-accused should have -- be valid or have probative value in relation to the other co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it is the law in Canada, in fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so too. More or less we have got similar. I don't know what the law is in Korea. I understand you well. This is basically what you're referring to. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, I think again it's something that, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This interesting issue of admissibility towards fellow accused is not a issue that will hold up the testimony and is an issue that can be briefed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly how I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell everyone that the policy of the Office of the Prosecutor is now that a statement can be used against fellow accused and it's up to the Court to decide what weight they give it. I think it's a more of a civil law view of things. In the Jokic case, there was no law on it and I went back on my -- my United States law and he's correct, we just went on what you're obviously familiar with. But in any event I welcome Mr. Ostojic's identifying a legal issue because that's the kind of legal issue I need to know about. Now, Mr. Ostojic has no standing in my view to argue the admissibility of Borovcanin's confession but that is an issue that his colleague may wish to take up. If it is an issue he wishes to take up, I need to know that so that I can be prepared because that's the kind of issue that could result in, if you find that his -- that the warnings were not sufficient, then Mr. Graham would not be called, obviously, or the excuse me, the statement would not come in. But if this is not something Mr. Lazarevic wishes to take on, then that's not the kind of issue I'm concerned about. But I do need to know if there is issues related to voluntariness, issues that sound to me like some kind of an attack on the credibility or the integrity of the Office of the Prosecutor, we need to have some idea of -- again, not the question but we do need something on that lines. Mr. Lazarevic also suggests the issue of admissibility of other co-accused is an issue he can discuss. Well, I don't think he has standing for himself to discuss that. So in any event, I would like -- I think we need to hear what legal issues, if any, Mr. Lazarevic has and after being aware of this issue for ten months, he either makes them tomorrow or they are waived and we go forward. We need more clarity than what I'm getting right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my understanding of what Mr. Lazarevic said is that he's prepared to give you broad insight into what he is contesting without going into further detail. That's my understanding. If I haven't read you well, Mr. Lazarevic, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour is completely right. That's exactly what I was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest is that you either say it now, in open court, so that it will go in the record, or you intimate it to the Prosecution after we adjourn. Either of the two. I would prefer if we have a clear statement now for the record. I think it would be sufficient if you just state on what basis you are contesting the admissibility of this interview or these interviews, whether it's on a question of voluntariness, whether it's violation of our particular rules, regulating, and in that case, in which part of the rule. I mean that's -- I think that can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so. I can do it openly now. All right. Besides two legal issues that I already mentioned, impact on other accused, it's really not a topic that I will cover, and the other one whether it is on Rule 65 ter list, the warning that was issued to Mr. Borovcanin was insufficient in our opinion. It was not according to rules, according to laws that Mr. Borovcanin was familiar of. Other thing is statutes that Mr. Borovcanin had during this interview. We believable that he was misled by the fact that he was -- well, that's basically what Mr. Ostojic said, that he was a potential suspect instead of being clear about his position, that he is a suspect when giving an interview and the rights that he has according to this. We believe that Mr. Borovcanin did not have adequate Defence and the preparation was not sufficient for this. Furthermore, we state that for one significant part of his interview, his counsel was not present at all. And if Your Honours could bear for one second with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and there is one more issue which is, of course, maybe interesting for Mr. McCloskey. We believe that during the interview, Mr. Borovcanin was directed to give certain answers, which he didn't intend to, and we will make it very clear once we are in a position to speak very openly, once Mr. Graham comes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough and should suffice for your purposes, Mr. McCloskey, unless you disagree. I don't think you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. That's very helpful. Most of those are legal grounds that are fairly common. And I don't see the -- some of the more traditional voluntary issues such as threats or inducements. I didn't hear that. I didn't hear anything directly improper aside from these arguments. So I thank my counsel for that. That does help us. And just one other issue that may be -- may be an issue, and all counsel might be able to help us. On the issue of admissibility of the statements against others, there are -- and of course I won't say what they are but there are some references to other co-accused and it would be our position that that would all come out during this interview and that we argue about admissibility later, this may be resolved by the Trial -- by the Appellate Chamber. There may be counsel that don't want any of that to come out, but I just say that because of -- if we can resolve that, if there are any people or any counsel that don't want or that are arguing that references should not come out in the interview, obviously we need to know that before we go into this so that we know what we are doing when we turn on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By come out my learned friend means adduced, rather than excised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean adduced, made open. Yeah, adduced. Adduced sounds good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can safely -- does anyone wish to address? Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that Mr. Miletic's Defence will file an objection to filing of this exhibit. I don't want to go into details but I would like to say that what has been said by Mr. McCloskey with regard to the countries where continental law is practised is simply not right. In such countries, the statements are given before an investigating judge, which is an entirely different matter. In other words, we will contest the admissibility with the interview with Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber with one more issue. During this break I was approached by Ms. Soljan and it seems we will resolve the issue of the transcripts of Mr. Borovcanin later this afternoon. So we most probably will have a transcript which is agreed by both sides here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I would agree with Ms. Fauveau. When we are talking investigative judge, that's the situation I was referring to. But -- and that is slightly different than lawyers and investigators so that-- I wasn't meaning to get that precise. But there is one thing that Mr. Thayer called my attention to and that was there was one of -- I think the fifth ground that someone in this interview may have pressured to witness to answer a certain way. And if that someone was me - and I can be a little pushy at times - we need to know about that. If that's their allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course if there is such thing, I will let Mr. McCloskey know in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just on the point that my learned friend made about standing, I disagree with him on that and I specifically, in light of his comment on page 74, lines 15 through 17, telling us what the change of position is, with the Office of the Prosecution, I think we clearly have standing to make the same or even different objection that Mr. Lazarevic may make with respect to the Mr. Borovcanin's interviews so I will be making those before the Court but the issue is not ripe for us until this moment to say that and we are still waiting to gets a completed transcript of those interviews. But I totally disagree with him that I do not have standing on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Your Honour, I could broadly speaking support that, Mr. Lazarevic at page 78, line 16, used the words both sides here. Of course, he means the Borovcanin Defence and the Prosecution. He doesn't mean the six other parties to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that needs to be repeated by anyone. Point taken. So one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've made it in time to communicate our position. We don't see any real need for any debate tomorrow at this point. I think the way we should approach it is to wait until Mr. Alistair Graham testifies, as scheduled on the 17th or thereabouts, and then the understanding is that all the submissions about admissibility in relation to Mr. Borovcanin and in relation to other accused will be heard afterwards, and then obviously we will need to decide on the admissibility issue, and the statements, the interviews will not be admitted in evidence until or unless we decide to, in which case, obviously, there will also be an appeal and whichever way we decide it actually there will be an appeal, I imagine. There is an appeal to be expected. All right? Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just housekeeping, Mr. Lazarevic's testimony, the Prosecution didn't have any exhibits. I don't know if the Defence did. Is that done? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. They had one document only. Oh, Mitar Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Kweku's witness. I don't think we finished the exhibits on Mr. Vanderpuye's witness, I think it was Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because he said he had none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When it comes to the witness Lazarevic, we don't have any exhibits for admission. The document P312, which was used in this witness's testimony, has already been admitted. We don't have any other documents, and I believe our list has already been submitted to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think we did state that before as well. I mean, it was certainly pointed out to me by Madam Registrar, and I think I raised it with Mr. Bourgon or with you. It was a document that had already been used and tendered by the Nikolic Defence team. So I don't think there is anything else. So that's it. All right. We'll resume you know when. But there is -- I don't think there is a need unless any one of you sees any significant need but we are certainly not going to meet to discuss whether it's on the 65 ter list or not on the 65 ter list. Thank you. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
